cards.title: Herring communicate by expelling gas from their rears
cards.body: To stay together in pitch-black ocean depths, Pacific and Atlantic herring communicate using high-frequency sounds produced by expelling gas from their anal ducts. Scientists dubbed these acoustic bursts Fast Repetitive Tick signals. Unlike human flatulence driven by digestion, herring force stored air from their swim bladders through their rear ends, alerting schoolmates to assemble safely without attracting night-hunting predators.

cards.title: The King of Sweden who ate himself to death on dessert
cards.body: King Adolf Frederick of Sweden died in 1771 after consuming an astonishingly massive royal feast. His dinner included lobster, caviar, sauerkraut, kippers, and champagne. However, the fatal blow came from dessert: he consumed 14 individual servings of semla, a rich Swedish pastry filled with almond paste and milk. The extreme overeating caused fatal digestive complications, earning him a place in history as the king who ate himself to death.

cards.title: Amazonian butterflies drink the tears of live turtles
cards.body: In the Amazon rainforest, butterflies are frequently seen swarming the eyes of sunbathing river turtles to drink their tears. This unusual behavior, known as lachryphagy, provides the insects with vital sodium and minerals that are extraordinarily scarce in their inland herbivorous diets. The turtles tolerate the fluttery visitors calmly, as the tears flow continuously and the gentle sipping causes them no physical harm.

cards.title: Ketchup was once sold in pharmacies as a cure-all pill
cards.body: In the 1830s, an American physician named John Cook Bennett claimed that tomatoes could cure ailments like indigestion, diarrhea, and jaundice. He published recipes for tomato ketchup and eventually concentrated the condiment into pill form, which was sold nationwide as a patent medicine. The ketchup pill craze thrived for a decade before collapsing when competing sellers were caught marketing ordinary pill substitutes containing zero tomatoes.

cards.title: Hagfish defend themselves by turning seawater into thick slime
cards.body: When threatened by a predator, the eel-like hagfish releases specialized proteins from glands along its body. Upon touching seawater, these proteins expand by over 10,000 times in volume within a fraction of a second, producing liters of sticky gel. This sudden slime explosion instantly clogs the gills of attacking fish, forcing them to choke and release the hagfish before it swims away completely unharmed.

cards.title: A mysterious dancing plague swept through Strasbourg in 1518
cards.body: In July 1518, a woman named Frau Troffea stepped into a street in Strasbourg and began dancing fervently. Within weeks, over 500 people had joined her, dancing uncontrollably day and night without music. Local authorities tragically encouraged more dancing by constructing stages and hiring musicians, believing victims needed to dance it out. Dozens of participants eventually collapsed and died from extreme exhaustion, stroke, or heart attack.

cards.title: One man hiccuped continuously for 68 years straight
cards.body: In 1922, an American farmer named Charles Osborne started hiccuping while attempting to weigh a hog. The hiccups did not stop until 1990, spanning an astonishing 68 years. Doctors estimated he hiccuped approximately 430 million times during his lifetime. Despite a rate of up to 40 hiccups per minute, Osborne led a full life, married twice, and fathered eight children before the mysterious condition suddenly vanished.

cards.title: Vatican City has the world's highest per-capita crime rate
cards.body: Statistical records consistently rank Vatican City as having the highest crime rate per person of any nation on Earth. However, this is a mathematical quirk caused by its tiny resident population of roughly 500 citizens compared to the tens of millions of tourists visiting St. Peter's Square each year. The vast majority of crimes recorded are minor pickpocketing incidents committed by visiting thieves against foreign tourists.

cards.title: Two Italian cities once fought a war over a stolen bucket
cards.body: In 1325, tensions between the rival Italian city-states of Modena and Bologna erupted into full-scale military conflict after Modenese soldiers raided Bologna and stole an oak bucket from a city well. The resulting Battle of Zappolino involved over 30,000 soldiers and resulted in more than 2,000 casualties. Modena won the battle and retained the wooden bucket, which remains proudly displayed in Modena's town hall to this day.

cards.title: Woodlice can absorb drinking water through their rears
cards.body: Woodlice, commonly known as pill bugs or roly-polies, are terrestrial crustaceans that face a constant risk of drying out. To stay hydrated, they do not rely solely on drinking through their mouths. Instead, woodlice can press specialized tube-like appendages called uropods, located at their rear end, against moist surfaces to draw up liquid water directly into their bodies through capillary action.

misconceptions.claim: Herring use digestion-related flatulence to communicate with each other.
misconceptions.explanation: Herring expel air stored in their swim bladders through their anal duct for communication, not digestive gas.

misconceptions.claim: Ketchup was originally commercialized in the United States as a stomach medicine.
misconceptions.explanation: In the 1830s, tomato ketchup was concentrated into pills and sold by doctors as a cure for indigestion.

misconceptions.claim: Vatican City is statistically the most dangerous country on Earth due to high violent crime rates.

misconceptions.claim: The 1325 War of the Bucket was fought solely because soldiers stole a wooden bucket.
misconceptions.explanation: While the stolen bucket became the symbolic cause and famous trophy, the war was triggered by decades of underlying political rivalry between Modena and Bologna.
